response: ## Finding `crime_00041` — **Oversized Raster**, `src/assets/hero-banner.png` > `byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB)` > `severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB` > `format: png` Severity `low`, confidence `0.95`, effort `quick`. ## Verdict: request changes, don't block 253.9 KB sits just over the bottom rung of the ladder — 27% above the 200 KB threshold, less than half of what would make it `medium`. That's not a merge-blocker on its own. What raises it above "nit" is *where* it lands: a landing-page hero is almost always the LCP element, so its bytes are on the critical path for the page's headline Core Web Vitals number, not amortised across lazy-loaded content. So: request changes, fix in this PR, don't hold the branch hostage. The finding's own `effort: quick` / `risk: low` supports that — it's a re-encode, not a rework. The real tell is `format: png`. A quarter-megabyte PNG for a hero strongly implies a photographic or gradient-heavy image shipped in a lossless container. That's a format mistake, not a "the image is too detailed" problem, and it's why I'd expect the fix to be dramatic rather than marginal. ## Recommended transformation **Caveat on dimensions:** the evidence gives bytes but no pixel dimensions for this asset — contrast `crime_00038`, where the detector reported `32 × 32 px` for the icon. So I can't derive the current size from the scan, and the target has to come from the render area. The rule, then the concrete numbers under a stated assumption: **Rule:** encode at the widest CSS width the image actually occupies × 2 for the highest-DPR variant, and let `srcset` serve smaller ones. Never ship one file sized for the largest possible viewport. **Assuming a standard full-bleed hero in a 1440px-max content shell:** | Variant | Dimensions | Serves | Byte target | |---|---|---|---| | `hero-banner-800.avif` | 800 × 450 | mobile 1x/2x | ~25 KB | | `hero-banner-1600.avif` | 1600 × 900 | desktop 1x, mobile 2x | ~60–80 KB | | `hero-banner-2560.avif` | 2560 × 1440 | desktop 2x / retina | ~150 KB | If the hero is a constrained banner strip rather than full-bleed (say it renders 1200 × 400), drop the whole set proportionally — 1200 and 2400 wide, and the 1x variant should land nearer 40 KB. Budget the *default* `src` at **≤ 100 KB**. That alone is a ~60% cut from today, before any dimension change. **Format: AVIF primary, WebP fallback, in a ``.** ```html ``` Why AVIF first: on photographic hero content it lands 20–30% below WebP at visually equivalent quality, and it handles gradients and smooth skies without the banding that pushes WebP encoders to spend bytes. Browser support is no longer the constraint it was — Chrome, Firefox, and Safari 16+ all decode it. Why keep WebP rather than going AVIF-only: it costs one extra build artifact and covers the residual older-Safari and embedded-webview traffic, and `` negotiates it at zero runtime cost. For a hero — the one image where a fallback miss is most visible — that's cheap insurance. Two caveats worth knowing rather than discovering: AVIF encoding is markedly slower than WebP, which matters if this runs per-build rather than once at asset-commit time; and if the "hero" is actually flat-colour artwork or contains rendered text, the AVIF advantage narrows and you should check whether it should be an SVG at all — which is exactly what the finding's `suggested_actions` hints at with "consider whether an SVG icon or CSS gradient would replace it entirely." Also add `fetchpriority="high"` and explicit `width`/`height`. Neither is what `crimes` flagged, but for an LCP hero they're worth more to the CWV number than the last 20 KB. ## One adjacent note Not this PR, but in the same `src/assets/` directory the scan reports `crime_00034` — `partner-logo.svg` carrying two base64-embedded rasters, at `high` severity with 0.95 confidence. That's a worse asset problem than the hero. If this PR is part of a broader asset pass, it's the one worth pulling forward.
